theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly shows that a public body needs a new organisational policy?
options: One officer prefers a different colour of file folder to others
A manager would like her staff to think better of her
Staff handle one issue in different ways, causing complaints
A supplier has started using a new delivery van

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy says what and why; a procedure gives the steps
A policy is optional for staff; a procedure is a law passed by Parliament
A policy is written by junior staff; a procedure by the Minister
They mean the same thing and the words can be swapped

questions.stem: A ministry's policy on the use of official vehicles conflicts with a law passed by Parliament. Which must be followed?
options: The policy, because it is more recent
Whichever the driver prefers
The policy, if the Permanent Secretary signed it
The law, and the policy must be corrected

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence for deciding what a new policy on staff overtime should cover?
options: A rumour heard in the canteen
Overtime records, audit findings and staff views
One manager's personal opinion

questions.stem: Before drafting a policy on staff use of social media, what should the policy officer research first?

What the officer's own friends post on their pages
The laws, service rules and policies that apply

questions.stem: Why should a policy officer consult the staff association or union before finalising a policy on shift patterns?
options: It affects members' conditions, and agreements may require it

So that the start of the policy can be put off for a full year
Because unions approve every policy in the public service

Definitions
Review date
Scope

questions.stem: Why should a policy name the officer or post that owns it?

So staff know whom to send all their leave forms to
So someone keeps it current and answers queries

questions.stem: A draft leave policy uses long sentences and legal terms, but most staff are not lawyers. What should the policy officer do?
options: Rewrite it plainly and test it on a few staff
Leave it as it is, because legal terms make it look official
Add more legal terms so that it covers every possible case
Attach a dictionary of legal terms to the back of the policy

options: So that it can replace the strategic plan altogether
So it is longer and more detailed than other policies
So the values can be rewritten to fit the new policy
So it supports, not undermines, the body's aims

questions.stem: A draft policy requires all staff to attend training on Saturdays. What should the policy officer check before approval?
options: Whether the canteen will be open on Saturdays for lunch
Its effect on staff with family or faith needs

questions.stem: A draft mileage policy pays officers J$65 per kilometre for official travel in their own vehicles. Twelve officers each travel about 800 km a month. What is the expected monthly cost?

options: Any officer who helped to draft it
The newest member of the administrative staff

questions.stem: Why should a draft policy on staff discipline be reviewed by the legal unit before approval?
options: To check it fits the law and service rules
To make it longer and more formal in tone

So that the legal unit can take over the HR work

questions.stem: Two versions of the leave policy are on the intranet, with different rules. What is the best fix?
options: Leave both online so that staff can choose which suits them
Keep one approved, numbered version; remove the other
Print both versions and file them together in one folder
Delete both and let managers decide case by case

questions.stem: What is the main use of a policy register?
options: To record daily staff attendance and lateness
To list approved suppliers and their prices
To store the complaints received from the public
To track each policy's owner and review date

options: March 2028
March 2027
March 2030
December 2025

questions.stem: A new policy on records management has been approved. Which launch approach is best?
options: Email the full policy once and assume all staff read it
Brief managers, then staff, and publish a summary
Pin it to a notice board in the basement store room
Tell staff about it only if they ask for it by name

questions.stem: Why might a public body ask each officer to sign that they have read and understood a new policy?
options: To prove that the officer can read and write
So that no training on the policy is ever needed
To show each officer received and understood it

questions.stem: Of 380 staff, 342 have signed to confirm they have read the new policy. What percentage is that?

options: What staff now do differently, with practice
The history of money and banking in Jamaica

How much it cost to print and bind the policy

questions.stem: After a new travel policy is approved, the old travel claim form no longer fits it. What should happen?
options: Keep using the old form until the stock runs out
Ask staff to write the new rules on the back of each
Update the form and procedure before launch

questions.stem: A policy sets office hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. An officer asks to work 7:30 to 3:30 to care for a parent. How should a well-written policy handle such cases?
options: Refuse every request, because the policy has no room to bend
Set an exceptions process: who approves and on what grounds
Let each officer choose their own hours without approval
Drop the policy for anyone who gives a good reason

questions.stem: Six months after a clean-desk policy started, how can the manager best check whether it is being followed?
options: Do spot checks and look at incident reports
Ask the policy owner whether she thinks it is working

questions.stem: An officer breaks the new policy on official vehicles by using one for private trips. How should the manager respond?
options: Ignore it, because the officer is popular with the team
Reprimand the officer loudly in front of the others
Change the policy so that private trips are allowed
Apply the breach process fairly and record it

questions.stem: Apart from the set review date, when should a policy be reviewed early?
options: When the policy owner goes on leave
When the font on the intranet changes
When a law changes or an incident shows it is not working
When a new photocopier arrives

questions.stem: What should a policy review mainly consider?
options: Only whether the policy is too long
Whether it still meets its purpose, the law and current practice
Only whether staff like the policy
Only the cost of printing it

questions.stem: A policy on fax machine use is still in the register, but the agency no longer uses fax machines. What should happen?
options: Withdraw it formally and record that it has been withdrawn
Leave it in place in case fax machines return
Delete it quietly with no record
Ask staff to keep following it

questions.stem: A draft promotion policy requires "at least ten years of service in Kingston". What is the main concern?
options: It is too short
It mentions Kingston

questions.stem: During consultation on a draft policy, staff send in 40 comments. What should the policy officer do with them?
options: Ignore every comment that she happens to disagree with
Accept every comment and change the draft for each
Weigh each, change the draft where justified, report back

questions.stem: A new agency policy changes how members of the public can request copies of records. Besides staff, who should be told, and how?
options: The public, through the website and service counters
Only the Minister, in a private letter from the CEO
No one outside, because the policy is an internal one

questions.stem: A draft policy on CCTV in a government office must respect the data protection law. Which provision fits the law's general purpose?
options: Recordings may be shared with anyone who asks for them
Signs inform people, and footage is kept only as needed
Cameras may be placed anywhere, including staff toilets
All recordings are to be kept forever in case of need

questions.stem: The officer who owns the purchasing card policy has retired. What should the organisation do?
options: Let the policy lapse
Ask the retired officer to keep it
Remove the policy from the intranet until someone asks

questions.stem: Managers in two divisions read a clause in the new leave policy differently. What is the best action?
options: Let each division keep its own reading of the clause
Ask all staff to vote on what the clause means
Ask the policy owner to rule, then fix the wording
Suspend the whole policy until the next review date

questions.stem: Before a new overtime policy, a unit paid J$1,200,000 a month in overtime. Six months later it pays J$900,000 a month. What is the reduction as a percentage?
Training on a new policy costs J$2,500 per person for 240 staff, plus J$150,000 for the trainer. What is the total cost?
Who should usually be on the working group that drafts a policy on staff health and safety?
options: Only the senior managers, so it can be done quickly
Managers, safety representatives, HR and legal
Only the legal unit, because it knows the law
An outside consultant working alone on the draft

questions.stem: A new remote-work policy lets staff use their own laptops, but the ICT security policy forbids it. What should the policy officer have done?
options: Ignored the ICT policy, because the new one is more recent
Asked staff which of the two policies they would prefer
Checked related policies and settled the conflict first
Removed the ICT security policy from the intranet

questions.stem: Once a policy is approved, who is mainly responsible for applying it in each unit?
options: The unit's manager
The policy officer alone
The Minister
The staff association

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows that a new customer complaints policy is working?
options: The policy has a modern cover and a new logo
Staff say that they have heard of the policy
The policy is longer and more detailed than the last
Complaints are settled faster and fewer recur

questions.stem: What is a policy framework in an organisation?
options: A wooden frame for hanging the mission statement
Rules for how policies are made, approved and reviewed
The list of staff who must sign each new policy
A diagram of the building used for fire drills

questions.stem: A draft policy needs 3 weeks of consultation, 2 weeks to revise and 4 weeks for approval. If drafting ends on 1 June, on about what date could it be approved?
options: 13 July
27 July
3 August
31 August

questions.stem: A senior manager asks the policy officer to word a new allowance policy so that only his own unit qualifies. What should she do?
options: Insist on fair criteria and raise it if pressed
Do it, because he is senior and can approve it
Do it quietly and tell no one about the request
Resign from the ministry at once in protest

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one-word term names the document that sets out the step-by-step method for carrying out a policy?
An agency updates a policy several times. Which two-word term names the controls, such as version numbers, dates and a change history, that stop staff working from an old copy?
Which document, binding on every public officer, covers matters such as gifts, conflicts of interest and political neutrality? (Three words.)
A policy approved in July 2026 is to be reviewed every two years. In what month and year is its next review due?
Of 250 officers, 215 completed training on a new policy. What percentage completed it?
What is the usual one-word heading of the policy section that explains terms used in it, such as "official vehicle"?
A policy allowance of J$4,500 a month is paid to 30 officers. What is the yearly cost, in J$?
What one word names an approved departure from a policy for a particular case, given by the authority the policy names?
What one-word term names an act that goes against a policy, such as using an official vehicle for a private trip?
What one word names advice that helps staff apply a policy but, unlike a rule, is not strictly binding?
A body has 48 policies, and 6 are past their review date. What percentage are overdue?
What one word describes a policy that has been formally taken out of force and removed from the current register?
What two-word term names the check, made while drafting, of how a policy will affect different groups such as women, people with disabilities or rural staff?
Overtime fell from J$800,000 to J$680,000 a month after a new policy. What is the reduction, as a percentage?
What one word names the internal website on which an organisation publishes its approved policies for staff?

essays.stem: A municipal corporation has no policy on staff use of social media, and two recent posts by staff have embarrassed the council. Describe the steps you would take to develop the policy, from confirming the need to approval.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the need and the scope with the CEO: the policy would cover all staff and councillors' support staff, on work and personal accounts where they mention the council. I would research the issue: the two incidents, the code of conduct, the public service rules on political neutrality and confidentiality, the data protection law and defamation in general terms, and policies used by other public bodies. I would then set up a small working group with HR, communications, ICT, a legal adviser and a staff representative. Together we would draft the policy using the corporation's template: purpose, scope, definitions, policy statements (for example, do not share confidential information, do not speak for the council unless authorised, be respectful), roles, how breaches are handled, related documents, owner and review date. I would check its effect on staff rights and fairness and test the wording on a few staff. The draft would go out for consultation to managers and the union, and I would record each comment and our response. The revised draft, with a short covering memo, would go to the authority named in the policy framework for approval.
markingPoints: Confirms need and scope with senior management
Researches incidents, laws and rules by purpose, and other bodies' policies
Forms a working group and drafts with a standard template
Checks fairness and plain wording
Consults, records responses and submits for formal approval

essays.stem: Describe the sections a well-structured organisational policy should contain, and explain the purpose of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A policy should begin with a title, number, version, approval date, owner and next review date, so readers know it is current and whom to ask. The purpose section states why the policy exists, linked to the organisation's aims or a legal duty. The scope sets out who and what it covers, for example all permanent and temporary staff at every office. Definitions explain terms that might be read in different ways. The policy statements are the heart of the document: short, clear rules using words such as "must" and "must not". Roles and responsibilities say what managers, staff and the policy owner must do. A section on compliance explains how the policy is monitored and what happens if it is breached, linked to the disciplinary process. Exceptions explain who can approve a departure and on what grounds. Related documents list the procedures, forms, other policies and laws that apply, named by their general purpose. A version history records changes. Together these sections make the policy clear, enforceable and easy to keep up to date.
markingPoints: Control details: title, version, owner, dates
Purpose and scope explained
Definitions and clear policy statements
Roles, compliance and exceptions explained
Related documents and version history, with the reason for each part

essays.stem: Compare policies, procedures and guidelines, and explain how they should fit together in a public body's policy framework, using an example.
essays.modelAnswer: A policy is a formal statement of what the organisation requires and why. It is approved at a senior level, applies widely and changes rarely. A procedure sets out the steps to carry out a policy: who does what, in what order and with which forms. It is approved by the policy owner or a manager and may change more often as systems change. A guideline gives advice and good practice to help staff apply the policy; it is not strictly binding, and staff may use judgement. In a good framework, each procedure and guideline links back to a policy, and none may contradict it, while the policy itself must fit the law and the public service rules. For example, an agency's records management policy might require that all official records are kept securely for the period the law and the records schedule set. The procedure would explain how to file, label and transfer records to the archive. A guideline might suggest how to name electronic files. Keeping these separate means the policy stays stable while procedures can be updated quickly.
markingPoints: Defines a policy correctly
Defines a procedure and a guideline correctly
Explains the hierarchy: law above policy, procedures and guidelines below
Gives a clear example showing how they link
Explains the benefit of keeping them separate

essays.stem: Explain how you would consult staff, managers, the union and other stakeholders on a draft policy on flexible working hours in a government agency, and how you would use their feedback.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first list who is affected: staff in each office, supervisors who arrange cover, the union or staff association, HR and payroll, the ICT unit if remote access is involved, and customers who rely on opening hours. I would plan the consultation with a clear period, for example three weeks, and explain what is still open to change. Methods would suit each group: a short summary and online survey for all staff, meetings with supervisors in each region, a formal meeting with the union in line with any agreement, and discussion with HR and payroll on how hours will be recorded. I would ask focused questions, such as which core hours customers need and what problems staff foresee. All comments would be recorded in a feedback log with the response to each: accepted, partly accepted or not accepted, with the reason. I would revise the draft, check the changes with the legal unit if needed, and report back to staff on what changed and why. This shows respect, improves the policy and builds support for it.
markingPoints: Identifies all affected groups, including customers
Plans a clear consultation period and what is open to change
Uses methods suited to each group, including formal union consultation
Records comments and responses in a feedback log
Revises the draft and reports back on changes and reasons

essays.stem: A draft policy will pay a monthly telephone allowance of J$3,000 to 85 field officers and J$5,000 to 15 supervisors. The budget allows J$3,600,000 a year. Calculate the yearly cost, compare it with the budget and recommend what the policy officer should do.
essays.modelAnswer: The field officers cost 85 × J$3,000 = J$255,000 a month, and the supervisors 15 × J$5,000 = J$75,000 a month, so the total is J$330,000 a month. A year costs J$330,000 × 12 = J$3,960,000. Checking: J$255,000 × 12 = J$3,060,000 and J$75,000 × 12 = J$900,000, which add up to J$3,960,000. This is J$360,000 over the J$3,600,000 budget, or 10% over. The policy cannot be approved as drafted unless more money is found. One option is to pay a flat J$3,000 to all 100 staff, which costs J$300,000 a month or exactly J$3,600,000 a year; but supervisors may make more calls, so the reason for a higher rate should be checked first. Another is to ask the finance unit for an extra J$360,000, with evidence of need. A third is to pay only staff whose work requires a phone. I would recommend checking call records, then setting rates that match real need within the budget, and stating in the policy that the rates will be reviewed each financial year.
markingPoints: Calculates J$330,000 a month and J$3,960,000 a year, with a check
Identifies the J$360,000 (10%) overspend
Gives realistic options, such as a flat J$3,000 rate (J$3,600,000) or more budget
Bases the recommendation on evidence of need
Builds a yearly rate review into the policy

essays.stem: Describe how you would launch a new records management policy across a ministry with offices in several parishes, so that staff understand it and follow it from the first day.
essays.modelAnswer: Before launch, I would make sure that everything staff need is ready: the approved policy on the intranet with a version number, updated procedures, file labels and transfer forms, and a short plain-language summary of what changes. I would brief directors and office managers first, because they must lead by example and answer questions in each parish office. Then I would hold short training sessions in each region, or online for small offices, showing how to file, label and store records and what to do with old files. Each officer would sign an acknowledgement that they have received and understood the policy. A named contact or help desk would answer questions in the first months, and a list of frequent questions would be shared. I would set a start date that allows time for the training, and agree with managers how they will check practice, for example by spot checks after one month. Feedback from the first weeks would be used to fix any unclear wording or procedure. Finally, I would report to senior management on training completed and early problems.
markingPoints: Prepares the policy, procedures, forms and summary before launch
Briefs managers first so they can lead and support
Trains staff in every location and gets acknowledgements
Provides ongoing support such as a contact and FAQs
Plans early compliance checks and feedback, and reports progress

essays.stem: Explain how an organisation should monitor compliance with its policies and deal with breaches fairly.
essays.modelAnswer: Each policy should say how compliance will be checked and who is responsible. Managers should check day-to-day practice in their own units, for example by reviewing records, observing work and discussing the policy in team meetings. The policy owner can use regular reports, such as overtime totals or complaint figures, and spot checks across units. Internal audit can test the most important policies on a risk basis. Staff should be able to report concerns safely, without fear of being victimised. When a possible breach is found, the manager should first establish the facts and give the officer a fair chance to explain. Minor first breaches caused by not understanding the policy are often best handled by guidance or training. Serious or repeated breaches should follow the disciplinary procedure, which must be applied consistently, in line with employment law and the public service rules. Every case should be recorded. Finally, patterns of breaches should be reported to the policy owner, because many breaches may mean the policy or its procedure is unclear or unworkable and needs review.
markingPoints: Assigns responsibility and methods for checking compliance
Uses reports, spot checks and audit on a risk basis
Provides safe ways for staff to report concerns
Handles breaches fairly: facts, a chance to explain, proportionate response, consistent with the rules
Records cases and uses patterns to review the policy

essays.stem: A ministry's policy register shows that many policies are out of date, some conflict with each other and staff do not know which version applies. Recommend a plan to bring the policy framework under control.
essays.modelAnswer: I would recommend a project led by a named senior officer and approved by the Permanent Secretary. First, a full inventory: collect every policy from the intranet, shared drives and filing cabinets, and record each in a single register with its owner, date, version and review date. Second, sort them: keep those that are current, merge those that overlap, mark conflicting ones for urgent review, and withdraw those that are obsolete, recording the withdrawal. Third, agree a policy framework that sets one template, the approval route for policies and procedures, version numbering, the review cycle, for example every three years or when a law changes, and who may publish documents. Fourth, prioritise the reviews by risk, starting with policies on finance, safety, data and staff conduct. Fifth, publish only approved, current versions in one place on the intranet, remove all other copies and tell staff where to find them. Finally, the register should be reported to senior management every quarter, showing policies overdue for review, so that the problem does not return.
markingPoints: Assigns senior ownership and approval
Makes a complete inventory in one register
Sorts policies: keep, merge, review or withdraw
Sets a framework with template, approval, versions and review cycle
Publishes one current version and reports on the register regularly

essays.stem: Explain why organisational policies must be consistent with the law and the public service rules, and describe how a policy officer can make sure a new policy is. Refer to laws only by their general purpose.
essays.modelAnswer: A public body can only act within its legal powers, and the law always takes priority over an internal policy. A policy that conflicts with the law, for example by allowing personal data to be shared without a proper reason or by denying leave that employment law gives, cannot be enforced. It could lead to legal challenge, complaints, financial loss and damage to public trust, and staff who follow it may be put at risk. Public officers are also bound by the public service rules and codes of conduct, so policies must fit them too. To make sure a new policy is consistent, the policy officer should list the laws and rules that apply, such as employment law, the data protection law, the access to information rules, safety law and the financial rules for public bodies, and read the relevant parts. She should check other policies for conflicts. She should ask the legal unit or the Attorney General's advisers, where needed, to review the draft. The related laws should be named in the policy, and the policy reviewed whenever a law changes.
markingPoints: Explains that law overrides policy and bodies act within their powers
Explains the risks of an unlawful policy
Includes the public service rules and codes
Describes checking laws and other policies, named by purpose
Uses legal review and reviews the policy when the law changes

essays.stem: A policy on staff overtime has been in place for two years. Explain how you would review it and decide whether to keep, change or withdraw it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by restating the policy's purpose, for example to control overtime costs while keeping services running. I would then gather evidence: overtime spending and hours before and since the policy, by unit; audit or compliance findings; the number of exceptions approved; complaints from staff or customers; and any changes in law, pay agreements or service hours. I would ask managers, staff and the union how the policy works in practice and whether any parts are unclear or unfair. I would compare the evidence with the purpose. If costs are controlled and services are maintained, with few problems, the policy can be kept, perhaps with small wording changes. If it is meeting its purpose in some units but causing problems in others, for example where shifts cannot be covered, I would recommend changes such as a clearer exceptions process. If the purpose has gone, for example because a new rostering system controls overtime, the policy might be merged or withdrawn. My recommendation, with reasons, would go to the approving authority, and the register would be updated with the new version and review date.
markingPoints: Restates the purpose and gathers evidence over time and by unit
Considers compliance, exceptions, complaints and changes in law or agreements
Consults managers, staff and the union
Decides keep, change or withdraw against the purpose, with reasons
Seeks approval and updates the register and review date

practical1.title: Draft an organisational policy with its procedure
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group an issue pack from a made-up public body (a ministry department, an agency or a municipal corporation), for example: staff use of official vehicles, clean desks and the security of paper files, staff use of social media, or flexible working hours. The pack contains a short description of the problem, two incident notes, an extract from the body's code of conduct, a list of the laws that apply described by their general purpose, and the body's policy template. As a group, prepare a policy pack containing: a one-page research note (the need, the laws and rules that apply, and related policies); a draft policy of no more than three pages using the template, with purpose, scope, definitions, policy statements, roles, breaches, exceptions, owner, version and review date; a one-page procedure or flowchart that puts the policy into practice; a short impact check on how the policy affects different groups of staff; and a one-page covering memo seeking approval. Give each member a named role: policy lead (keeps time, writes the memo and assembles the pack), researcher (writes the research note), drafter (writes the policy statements and definitions), procedure writer (prepares the procedure or flowchart), and impact and legal checker (writes the impact check and checks the draft against the laws and rules listed). In a group of four, the policy lead also writes the impact check. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes.
materials: Issue pack and policy template from the assessor
Computers with word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The flipchart with roles, timetable and the issues drawn from the pack
The draft policy, showing the control details (owner, version, review date)
The impact check and the legal check notes
The covering memo and the assembled policy pack
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Research note identifies the need and the laws and rules by general purpose
Policy follows the template and its statements are clear, short and enforceable
Procedure matches the policy and gives clear steps and responsibilities
Impact check identifies groups who may be affected and suggests fair adjustments
Draft does not conflict with the laws, rules or code given
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up public body, names and incidents; keep the pack confidential to the group and assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Consult on a draft policy and prepare its launch pack
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a two-page draft policy from a made-up public body (for example a policy on overtime, on records management or on telephone allowances) with a cost table and role cards for a consultation meeting. As a group: (1) check the cost table and work out the yearly cost of the policy, checking every sum twice; (2) hold a 25-minute consultation meeting as a role play, with members playing the policy owner, a manager, a union representative and a staff member, using the role cards; (3) record every comment in a feedback log with the response (accepted, partly accepted or not accepted) and the reason; (4) revise the draft with the changes shown, and give it a new version number and review date; (5) prepare a launch pack: a one-page plain-language summary for staff, an acknowledgement form, a one-hour training outline and an entry for the policy register. Give each member a named role: chairperson and policy owner (runs the meeting and approves the changes), cost analyst (checks the cost table, checked by another member), feedback recorder (keeps the feedback log), editor (revises the draft and updates the version details), and launch officer (prepares the summary, acknowledgement form, training outline and register entry). In a group of four, the editor also prepares the register entry. Every member must speak in the meeting. Photograph each stage and hand in the cost check, feedback log, revised draft and launch pack.
materials: Draft policy, cost table and role cards from the assessor
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet software, and a printer
Feedback log and policy register templates (optional)
photos: The cost check with every sum shown and the second check marked
The consultation meeting in progress (notes and table only if anyone prefers no face)
The completed feedback log with responses and reasons
The revised draft showing the changes, the new version number and review date
The plain-language summary and the acknowledgement form
The training outline and the policy register entry
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
